newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-High exports, low imports cut API heat build.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-High exports, low imports cut API heat build.

text.p: A meager build in distillate stocks in the latest American Petroleum Institute (API) report, exacerbated by low imports and voluminous exports, helped push U.S. oil prices higher late Tuesday.

Distillates for October delivery led the way, rising by 0.50 to 0.75 cent on ACCESS to about 66.30 cents a gallon, after API said stocks rose by just 235,000 barrels to 112 million barrels -- 21.5 million below year-ago levels.
"Overall the report looks bullish for distillates and crude and neutral for gasoline," said Tom Bentz, analyst at ING Derivatives Clearing in New York.
October crude on ACCESS was up by about 10 cents to about $23.45 a barrel, while October gasoline was steady to 0.25 cent higher after endeing at 62.74 cents a gallon on NYMEX.
Crude stocks fell by two million barrels to 307.7 million barrels despite an import-led 2.3 million Gulf Coast rise.
Total gasoline stocks rose by 434,000 barrels to 191.8 million, helped by a solid 2.4 million Gulf Coast build as well as relatively high imports of 341,000 barrels per day.
Analysts also said they saw bullishness in the fact crude stocks built despite the 0.3 percentage point rise in refinery utilization rates that brought run rates to 95 percent.
But the lack once again of a voluminous distillate rise was the report's most distinct feature.
"Whether or not the build was disappointing depends on what side of the market you're on. But the clear winner tonight will be heat-to-crude crack spreads," said one trader.
The October heat-to-crude crack was up to $4.46 a barrel on ACCESS after settling at $4.24 during the NYMEX session.
Traders said Tuesday the lack of meaningful builds in stocks of middle distillates in the U.S. in the run up to winter is being exacerbated by increased exports to other regions, particularly Europe.
"It is definitely starting to move that way (from U.S. to Europe)," said Jeff Goetz, a tanker broker at Seabrokers in New York.
He said there were a number of cargoes fixed to steam from the U.S. and the Caribbean last and another surge of ship inquiries early this week.

"This (traffic) was virtually non-existant on a regular basis" until a few weeks ago, said a broker at Poten, another shipbroking firm. He said that at least another two ships were booked late on Monday to bring nearly 100,000 tonnes of middle distillate to Europe.

"We did confirm that a number of cargoes were leaving either from the East Coast for the Gulf Coast and going over to Europe," said Linda Abramo, an analyst at Energy Security Analysis Inc. in Washington.
The reason for the trans-Atlantic traffic can be seen in the price charts of European and U.S. heating oil/gas oil, Abramo points out.

The strong European market, accounted for by a combination of low stocks (20 million barrels below last year) and a European Union rule change requiring lower sulphur content, has kept the premium for gas oil there at an average of more than two cents a gallon since early September.
Abramo says the rule-of-thumb for the market is that it starts to become profitable to ship from the U.S. to Europe when the European premium moves above 1.5 cents a gallon.
"We are figuring that through October you are probably going to see some high prices in Europe and the spread can work on occasion. After that it will probably calm down," said Abramo.
